Okay.
My name is Helen Dallas. I'm from the Freshwater Research Centre based in Cape
Town, South Africa. The title of my talk is Biodiversity
Data at Your Fingertips. I'll be sharing with you details of the
freshwater biodiversity information systems that we have developed for South
Africa and scaled up for Africa. And I'm presenting on
behalf of my co-authors, Jeremy Shelton,
Nazli Little from the Freshwater Research Centre, as well as
my colleagues, Dimos Trikomkos and Tim Sutton from
CartoSA.
All of this work has been funded by the JRS Biodiversity Foundation.
Freshwater biodiversity data are essential for monitoring ecosystem
change, for informing conservation, and for supporting
evidence-based management of freshwater ecosystems.
However, such data are often fragmented, both across
institutions and regions,
often inaccessible, and thus valuable data are very difficult to discover
or poorly integrated across scales and taxonomic groups.
Data are therefore often underused in decision-making,
and yet the threats to freshwater ecosystems continue to grow.
The Freshwater Biodiversity Information System, FBIS,
and FBIS Africa platforms, developed for South Africa
and for Africa respectively, respond
directly to this challenge by connecting data,
people, and decisions.
The process to develop FBIS for South Africa started back in
2017. A user-centered approach was
followed to allow us to design backwards based on the
needs of the end users.
The design and functionality of FBIS have thus been shaped by
key user groups, including, but not limited to
water resource managers, conservation managers and
planners, researchers and scientists,
environmental consultants, and policymakers.
The result is a powerful visual data-rich
system designed to host, share, and
explore freshwater biodiversity data in South
Africa.
The platform currently holds more than 14 million occurrence
records of freshwater taxa on the platform.
FBIS has eight biodiversity modules, including
fish, annelids, invertebrates,
wetland and riparian plants, algae,
wetland birds, and water-dependent mammals and
reptiles. We have a growing freshwater community
with 1,648 registered users
on the platform, and these users are currently
actively uploading and downloading data
from the platform.
Importantly, in South Africa, we are using freshwater data from
FBIS to support science conservation
and management of freshwater ecosystems in the country.
So what data tools have we developed in FBIS
to turn biodiversity records into usable information?
Firstly, there is a taxonomic management system
that uses the taxonomic backbone of the global
biodiversity information facility to provide the
taxonomic information for each taxon on the
platform. Going forward, in collaboration with FADA,
we will be integrating these platforms so that they all speak to each other.
There are also links
to the IUCN for global conservation status for
those species that have been red-listed.
Occurrence data is the primary currency of the platform, and a
range of queries and filters have been developed to allow the
extraction of subsets of data based on a user
query or filter application.
For example, a range of spatial filters and temporal
filters are available, and these can be applied
independently or in combination to provide very
powerful filtering opportunities for extracting data.
There are a number of visual spatial layers that have been
served on the various platforms, and these are specifically for
visualizing the data, and these include, for example,
layers related to management, catchments,
ecoregions, vegetation, climate,
protected areas, and conservation layers.
This is just an example of some of the layers on the platforms.
We've also developed a range of standardized dashboards
which translate the occurrence records into
easy-to-use information. This information includes
maps, overview information, graphs,
metadata, and other visual tools for displaying
data. Importantly, every single occurrence record
on the FBIS and FBIS Africa platforms have
associated with it metadata to allow for
citation and attribution.
All graphs and data may be downloaded for including in reports and
for further analysis.
In designing the FBIS, the intention was to design it in a
way that the platform could serve not
only the needs of the FBIS South Africa community, but
could serve as an underlying engine for other information
systems.
And this was possible by separating the underlying engine from
the data, and this has enabled FBIS South Africa
to be modified and deployed for other platforms, including
non-freshwater platforms, as well as being scaled up for
Africa.
Therefore, FBIS
Africa is a move from national to continental scale,
and it is rapidly expanding in both data coverage and user
uptake.
The ambition
for FBIS Africa is a stronger community of freshwater biodiversity
data users and contributors across Africa
for the betterment of Africa's freshwater ecosystems and people.
Both FBIS and the FBIS Africa platforms
interoperate with global biodiversity infrastructures,
including GBIF and the IUCN Red List of Threatened
Species, and in this way, they contribute to a more connected
and accessible freshwater data ecosystem.
By combining regional expertise, open
infrastructure,
interoperable data workflows, and powerful biodiversity
analysis tools, FBIS and FBIS-Africa demonstrate
how community-driven information systems can support fair
biodiversity data mobilization and translate
biodiversity knowledge into
actionable conservation and management
outcomes.
One information ecosystem, multiple scales.
From the level of site, to catchment, to national,
to continental, to global.
Each level adds value while remaining connected
to the others.
And thus regional expertise can therefore contribute to
continental and global biodiversity knowledge.
A multi-tenant model has been used for improving
sustainability of all platforms, with each
tenant onboarded experiencing independent
governance and customized branding of their platforms.
Those of you who have been involved in development of information systems in the
past know the challenge associated with
sustainability, both in terms of funding but also in terms
of data.
There are benefits to be had
from this multi-tenant model, and these include
beneficial cost savings,
improved technical infrastructure,
platform improvements shared across all tenants,
and increased resilience across all platforms.
Reflecting back on the FBIS and FBIS-Africa journeys,
I'd like to share with you five design principles that we feel
demonstrate the success of the FBIS
model.
Firstly,
stakeholder co-design promotes uptake and value.
Interoperability with systems such as GBIF and IUCN
multiplies the impacts of the platform.
Open access
enables collaboration and innovation,
and sustained support and partnerships were an
essential ingredient to the success of both FBIS and
FBIS-Africa.
The incorporation of multi-tenancy increases resilience
and fosters sustainability of all the platforms.
So why does this matter for freshwater biodiversity?
Freshwater ecosystems support biodiversity, people, and
economies. So it's not just about freshwater biodiversity.
There's a very strong link to people and economies.
Data-informed decisions are critical in the face of rapid
change,
and open accessible data empower diverse
users across Africa and beyond.
Stronger data ecosystems enable a more resilient and
sustainable future for all.
In conclusion,
open, interoperable, and user-driven biodiversity
information systems can transform freshwater data
into action.
Thank you for your attention.
Thank you very much, Helen, in case you hear me.
